summary: For ages 9–11: Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into large tectonic plates that ride on hotter, softer rock beneath (the asthenosphere) and move very slowly — a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Over many millions of years this adds up to continents drifting huge distances, and the volcano/earthquake belts (the Ring of Fire) line up along the plate edges. Core goals: the crust is a cracked shell of plates (not one solid ball), plates ride on hot but mostly SOLID rock that flows slowly (not liquid lava), and the motion is imperceptibly slow yet powerful over time. The strongest activity lets learners enact slow plate movement and fast-forward time; map-reveal, sorting/check, and globe views are supporting scaffolds with stated limits.
misconceptions: The ground is one solid, unbroken, unmoving ball of rock (it is a cracked shell of moving plates).
Plates float on liquid lava or on the molten core (they ride on hot but mostly SOLID rock that flows very slowly).
Plates move fast enough to feel (they move a few cm/year — imperceptible, but enormous over millions of years).
Plates are the same as continents (a plate can carry both continent and ocean floor; plate edges are not coastlines).
The plates are small pieces like a cracked eggshell everywhere (there are a handful of very large plates plus smaller ones).

activities.title: Moving rafts and the time machine
steps: Start with a world map that looks like solid, unbroken ground, then watch (or trigger) it crack into its plate jigsaw of a handful of large plates plus smaller ones.
Grab and nudge a plate and notice it barely budges — representing only a few centimetres a year, far too slow to see in real time.
Use a time control to fast-forward through tens to hundreds of millions of years and watch those tiny creeps add up until continents move thousands of kilometres.

Toggle on an overlay of volcano and earthquake dots and check that most of them line up along the plate EDGES rather than being scattered randomly across the map (a few, like Hawaii's volcanoes, are in the middle of a plate).
Say in your own words: the ground is a set of moving rafts riding on hot, mostly solid rock that flows very slowly (not liquid lava), and most hazards cluster where plate edges meet.
activities.insight: Solid-looking ground is actually a set of slowly moving plates riding on hot, mostly-solid rock that flows very slowly; the motion is imperceptible day to day but enormous over millions of years, and it explains why volcanoes and earthquakes cluster along plate edges.

activities.title: Label the plate jigsaw and reveal the facts
steps: Explore a labelled world plate map; identify the major plates by name.
Reveal, for a chosen plate, that it rides on hot but mostly solid rock (not liquid lava) that flows slowly, and moves roughly a few centimetres per year.
Open a 'How fast do these move?' reveal and connect the rate to fingernail growth (the fastest plates move closer to how fast hair grows).
Drill into a cross-section showing a plate riding on slowly-flowing hot mantle rock beneath.
activities.insight: The crust is divided into named plates of various sizes, each riding on hot but mostly solid rock that flows slowly (not liquid lava) and moving at a fingernail-slow rate.

activities.title: Feel how slow and soft: analogies for rate and flow
steps: Compare plate speed to fingernail growth (a few cm per year; the fastest plates move closer to how fast hair grows, roughly 10–15 cm per year) using a slider or picking the right scale from millimetres to metres per year.
Discuss a slow-flow analogy — very stiff toffee, thick custard, or ice creeping in a glacier — to picture solid rock that can flow over long times.

Calculate roughly: at a few cm per year, how far would a plate travel in a million years? (A few cm × a million ≈ tens of kilometres; thousands of kilometres of continental drift build up only over tens to hundreds of millions of years.)
activities.insight: A few centimetres per year feels like nothing, but multiplied over millions of years it produces huge movement — roughly tens of kilometres per million years, scaling to thousands of kilometres only over tens to hundreds of millions of years; and 'floating on softer rock' means riding on hot but mostly solid rock that flows slowly, not liquid lava.

activities.title: Check and sort what is true of plates
steps: Answer: What do the plates ride on? (Hot but mostly solid rock that flows slowly — not a sea of liquid molten rock.)
Choose the correct speed scale for plate movement (a few cm per year, like fingernail growth).

Sort statements into true/false of plates — e.g., 'plates are the same as continents' (false), 'a plate can carry both continent and ocean floor' (true), 'the ground is one solid unmoving ball' (false).
activities.insight: Consolidates the broken-shell idea, the ride-on-soft-rock fact, and the very slow rate, while surfacing the liquid-lava and plate-equals-continent misconceptions.

activities.title: Wrap the plates around a globe (companion view)
steps: Spin a globe showing the plate jigsaw wrapping the whole Earth, and watch slow drift across its curved surface.
Compare the globe view with the flat map to see how the same plates cover a sphere.
activities.insight: Plates cover the whole spherical Earth, not just a flat map; the jigsaw wraps a ball.

checkQuestion: Someone says, 'The continents have always been exactly where they are now — solid ground can't move.' Is that true? What are the tectonic plates, what are they moving on, and how fast do they move?
checkAnswer: Not true. Earth's crust is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. They rest on hotter, softer (partly-melted) rock in the mantle that can slowly flow, and they move very slowly — only a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Over millions of years that adds up to continents moving huge distances.
